Higher entropy inputs reduce context stability, with stability scores declining from 0.91 for low entropy to 0.67 for high entropy.
Positional encoding stability decreases with longer sequences, from 0.93 at 50 tokens to 0.66 at 500 tokens.
papers.limitation:
Model selection confined to a single open-source LLM architecture limits generalizability across different model structures.
Experimental conditions constrained by synthetic input generation lack the variability inherent to natural language environments.
future_direction: Cross-model CFD comparisons to evaluate whether drift patterns are consistent across architectures.
Expanding experimental setups to include more diverse linguistic datasets to better mirror authentic conversational data.
Developing more granular CFD metrics to capture subtle drift variations, such as at the layer-wise or attention-head level.
papers.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence have led to models capable of generating highly coherent language, yet limitations in retaining contextual alignment across extended inputs remain challenging. Contextual Feature Drift (CFD) emerges as a significant yet underexplored phenomenon, describing how sequential input dynamics affect contextual consistency within model outputs. This paper investigates CFD within an open-source transformer-based model, employing controlled synthetic data sequences to analyze context retention as influenced by factors such as input length, semantic similarity, entropy variability, and temporal intervals. Experimental results reveal that extended input lengths, lower semantic similarity, and high-entropy sequences exacerbate CFD, demonstrating quantifiable declines in context retention. Positional encoding and attention allocation metrics provide further insight into feature drift, showing potential vulnerabilities for applications relying on consistent sequential context, including conversational AI and recommendation systems. The study highlights the criticality of mitigating CFD for enhancing model reliability, positing that strategic adjustments to LLM architectures and training methods may support more robust applications requiring sustained context fidelity. Through this investigation, the findings contribute a foundational understanding of CFD, establishing its relevance for future research and LLM development.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of knowledge neurons and a gradient-based attribution method to identify them in pretrained Transformers, demonstrating their role in storing factual knowledge and enabling model editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons (knowledge neurons) within feed-forward networks, and these neurons can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed attribution method are positively correlated with the expression of specific factual knowledge.
Suppressing or amplifying the activation of identified knowledge neurons significantly decreases or increases the probability of the correct answer, respectively.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts expressing their corresponding fact than by control prompts.
Knowledge neurons can be used to update or erase specific factual knowledge in the model with minimal impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Examines knowledge neurons based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain underexplored.
Focuses on factual knowledge for ease of evaluation, though the method is applicable to other knowledge types.
Uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Explore interactions between knowledge neurons.
Extend the method to other types of knowledge beyond factual knowledge.
Extend to multi-word blanks in cloze queries.
Investigate knowledge neurons in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus. In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: How the Brain Represents Language and Answers Questions? Using an AI System to Understand the Underlying Neurobiological Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the brain represent language and answer questions? The paper investigates this by proposing a framework of neural mechanisms inspired by an AI question-answering system.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework of 12 neurally plausible mechanisms that could implement language-based question answering in the brain, inspired by the AI system START.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that known or plausible neural mechanisms are sufficient to perform the complex cognitive function of question answering, providing a first view of how this could be implemented by the brain.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a two-stage chunking process to convert temporal language sequences into spatial patterns for storage and recall.
Suggests working memory buffers organized by theta and gamma oscillations can hold up to 7 triplets (subject-verb-object units).
Describes a retrieval process where the episodic long-term memory network finds the stored memory most similar to a question, even with different word order.
Introduces neural mechanisms for pointers to handle complex sentences with embedded clauses.
Proposes mechanisms for conceptual alignment and comparison to answer yes/no and WH-questions.
future_direction: Development of a complete functional architecture integrating the proposed mechanisms.
Further reinterpretation of the model in terms of potential interactions with other systems such as the visual and auditory systems.
Considering the viewpoint of embodied cognition to obtain other neural mechanisms supporting language processing.
papers.abstract: To understand the computations that underlie high-level cognitive processes we propose a framework of mechanisms that could in principle implement START, an AI program that answers questions using natural language. START organizes a sentence into a series of triplets, each containing three elements (subject, verb, object). We propose that the brain similarly defines triplets and then chunks the three elements into a spatial pattern. A complete sentence can be represented using up to 7 triplets in a working memory buffer organized by theta and gamma oscillations. This buffer can transfer information into long-term memory networks where a second chunking operation converts the serial triplets into a single spatial pattern in a network, with each triplet (with corresponding elements) represented in specialized subregions. The triplets that define a sentence become synaptically linked, thereby encoding the sentence in synaptic weights. When a question is posed, there is a search for the closest stored memory (having the greatest number of shared triplets). We have devised a search process that does not require that the question and the stored memory have the same number of triplets or have triplets in the same order. Once the most similar memory is recalled and undergoes 2-level dechunking, the sought for information can be obtained by element-by-element comparison of the key triplet in the question to the corresponding triplet in the retrieved memory. This search may require a reordering to align corresponding triplets, the use of pointers that link different triplets, or the use of semantic memory. Our framework uses 12 network processes; existing models can implement many of these, but in other cases we can only suggest neural implementations. Overall, our scheme provides the first view of how language-based question answering could be implemented by the brain.

papers.title: A Hopfieldian View-based Interpretation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: For zero-shot CoT, why does prompting the model with 'let's think step by step' significantly impact its outputs? For few-shot CoT, why does providing examples before questioning the model substantially improve its reasoning ability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework based on the Hopfieldian view to interpret Chain-of-Thought reasoning, enabling error localization and control to correct reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides intuitive and interpretable analysis for CoT reasoning, which is helpful in tracing and controlling errors made during the CoT process, rectifying reasoning paths, and enhancing transparency.
papers.key_findings:
The framework can decipher the inner workings of CoT reasoning.
It provides reasoning error localization by reading concept-specific representations.
It controls the reasoning direction to rectify errors and improve accuracy.
The approach answers why zero-shot and few-shot CoT prompts improve reasoning.
Experimental results on seven datasets across three tasks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness.
papers.limitation: The current problem formulation is primarily focused on text data.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-modal scenarios.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) holds a significant place in augmenting the reasoning performance for large language models (LLMs). While some studies focus on improving CoT accuracy through methods like retrieval enhancement, yet a rigorous explanation for why CoT achieves such success remains unclear. In this paper, we analyze CoT methods under two different settings by asking the following questions: (1) For zero-shot CoT, why does prompting the model with "let's think step by step" significantly impact its outputs? (2) For few-shot CoT, why does providing examples before questioning the model could substantially improve its reasoning ability? To answer these questions, we conduct a top-down explainable analysis from the Hopfieldian view and propose a Read-and-Control approach for controlling the accuracy of CoT. Through extensive experiments on seven datasets for three different tasks, we demonstrate that our framework can decipher the inner workings of CoT, provide reasoning error localization, and control to come up with the correct reasoning path.

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Discourse structure interacts with reference but not syntax in neural\n language models
papers.research_question: Does discourse structure (implicit causality) influence reference and syntactic processing in neural language models, and how does this compare to human behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models learn a representational distinction for implicit causality that influences reference resolution but not syntactic attachment, while LSTM language models fail to learn such a distinction, revealing a mismatch between learned representations and behavior in language models.
papers.conclusion: Language models can learn discourse structure (implicit causality) from text, but they do not consistently use this knowledge in behavior, especially for syntactic processing, indicating limitations in how they acquire and utilize linguistic abstractions.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM language models show no influence of implicit causality on reference or syntax.
TransformerXL shows partial implicit causality representation, influencing reference but not syntax.
GPT-2 XL shows robust implicit causality effects on reference, matching human behavior, but not on syntax.
Transformers encode implicit causality in representations for both reference and syntax, but this knowledge does not affect syntactic behavior.
Both transformer models show a strong preference for local agreement in syntax, overriding discourse effects.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to unidirectional models and specific architectures, so mechanistic claims about the relationship between learned linguistic knowledge and model configurations are cautioned.
The representational similarity measure (Pearson's r) may not be optimal for capturing the relevant distinctions, especially for LSTM models.
The models may be unable to learn the syntactic operation of attachment, as suggested by the erasure of number agreement in final layers.
future_direction: Investigate the role of training objectives, such as predicting coherence relations instead of next-word prediction.
Explore the exact role of training data and model architecture in learning linguistic interactions.
Cross-linguistic studies to further understand the limitations of language models in learning syntax.
papers.abstract:
Language models (LMs) trained on large quantities of text have been claimed
to acquire abstract linguistic representations. Our work tests the robustness
of these abstractions by focusing on the ability of LMs to learn interactions
between different linguistic representations. In particular, we utilized
stimuli from psycholinguistic studies showing that humans can condition
reference (i.e. coreference resolution) and syntactic processing on the same
discourse structure (implicit causality). We compared both transformer and long
short-term memory LMs to find that, contrary to humans, implicit causality only
influences LM behavior for reference, not syntax, despite model representations
that encode the necessary discourse information. Our results further suggest
that LM behavior can contradict not only learned representations of discourse
but also syntactic agreement, pointing to shortcomings of standard language
modeling.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What are the precise training dynamics during the emergence of induction heads for in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a simple, interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing induction heads and proves that training dynamics are constrained to a low-dimensional subspace, with only three parameters accounting for the emergence.
papers.conclusion: This work shows how induction heads emerge in an ICL task and paves the way for a better theoretical understanding of transformer learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrices of an induction head have a simple structure described by three pseudo-parameters (α3, β2, γ3).
Training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace, and only three dimensions are necessary for the induction head to emerge.
The emergence time of the induction head is quadratic in the context length (Θ(N^2)).
The three parameters emerge in a specific order: γ first, then β, then α.
The emergence of the induction head is self-contained, unaided by the other parameters.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope is limited to a disentangled, attention-only transformer; production models with LayerNorm, MLPs, and additive residual streams may have different dynamics.
Theoretical results assume orthonormal inputs and zero initialization, which may not hold in practice and could alter emergence times.
The study uses a simplified ICL task (exact matching of item-label pairs), not natural language with its complexities.
future_direction: Exploring how data distributional properties like burstiness modulate the effective context length and emergence.
Investigating other means of reducing effective context length, such as special positional embeddings.
Applying a similar approach to study other phenomena like the in-context vs. in-weights learning trade-off, abrupt learning, or other transformer circuits.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant architecture for natural language processing. Part of their success is owed to a remarkable capability known as in-context learning (ICL): they can acquire and apply novel associations solely from their input context, without any updates to their weights. In this work, we study the emergence of induction heads, a previously identified mechanism in two-layer transformers that is particularly important for in-context learning. We uncover a relatively simple and interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing the induction head. We theoretically explain the origin of this structure using a minimal ICL task formulation and a modified transformer architecture. We give a formal proof that the training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace of the parameter space. Empirically, we validate this constraint while observing that only 3 dimensions account for the emergence of an induction head. By further studying the training dynamics inside this 3-dimensional subspace, we find that the time until the emergence of an induction head follows a tight asymptotic bound that is quadratic in the input context length.

papers.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.research_question: Do chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations faithfully represent the true reasons for a model's prediction, or can they be systematically unfaithful by being influenced by biasing features not mentioned in the explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations can be plausible yet systematically unfaithful; models can be influenced by biasing features (e.g., option order or suggested answers) without mentioning them in their explanations, rationalizing incorrect or biased predictions.
papers.conclusion: CoT explanations can be misleading, increasing trust in LLMs without guaranteeing safety. Building transparent systems requires either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.
papers.key_findings:
Adding biasing features (e.g., 'Answer is Always A' or 'Suggested Answer') heavily influences model CoT predictions on BBH tasks, causing accuracy to drop by up to 36%.
When biasing features point to incorrect answers, models frequently alter their CoT explanations to justify those incorrect bias-consistent predictions, sometimes with sound reasoning.
On the social bias task (BBQ), models give plausible unfaithful explanations that support answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of stereotypes, using weak evidence inconsistently.
papers.limitation:
Manual evaluation of explanations is costly and subjective.
The study is limited to two models (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0) and a subset of tasks.
The biasing features used are simple and may not cover all ways explanations could be unfaithful.
future_direction: Improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts (e.g., training objectives that incentivize faithful explanations).
Abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods for model transparency and explainability.
Extending the evaluation to more models, tasks, and biasing features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve strong performance on many tasks by producing step-by-step reasoning before giving a final output, often referred to as chain-of-thought reasoning (CoT). It is tempting to interpret these CoT explanations as the LLM's process for solving a task. This level of transparency into LLMs' predictions would yield significant safety benefits. However, we find that CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. We demonstrate that CoT explanations can be heavily influenced by adding biasing features to model inputs--e.g., by reordering the multiple-choice options in a few-shot prompt to make the answer always "(A)"--which models systematically fail to mention in their explanations. When we bias models toward incorrect answers, they frequently generate CoT explanations rationalizing those answers. This causes accuracy to drop by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard, when testing with GPT-3.5 from OpenAI and Claude 1.0 from Anthropic. On a social-bias task, model explanations justify giving answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of these social biases. Our findings indicate that CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading, which risks increasing our trust in LLMs without guaranteeing their safety. Building more transparent and explainable systems will require either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.

papers.title: Mechanism Shift During Post-training from Autoregressive to Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: Does post-training autoregressive models into masked diffusion models induce genuine bidirectional reasoning mechanisms, or do they merely repackage autoregressive heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: Post-training autoregressive models into masked diffusion models induces a task-dependent mechanism shift, preserving autoregressive circuitry for local causal tasks but rewiring for global planning tasks with increased early-layer processing and distributed semantic integration.
papers.conclusion: Masked diffusion post-training induces a task-dependent mechanism shift, preserving autoregressive mechanisms for local causal reasoning while reorganizing them for more globally integrated, non-sequential reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
For the local causal task (IOI), MDMs largely preserve the autoregressive circuitry inherited from their ARM initializations.
For the global reasoning task (Countdown), MDMs show low circuit overlap with ARMs and a strong shift in computation to earlier layers (lower Center of Gravity).
MDMs transition from sharp, localized component specialization (as in ARMs) to distributed semantic integration across components.
At the neuron level, early layers in MDMs exhibit reduced task-specific selectivity and more uniform activation profiles compared to ARMs.
Diffusion post-training reorganizes internal computation rather than merely adjusting parameters, supporting non-sequential global planning.
papers.limitation:
The study is confined to two benchmark tasks (IOI and Countdown), limiting generalizability.
The circuits identified are task-specific findings rather than universal signatures of autoregressive or masked diffusion models.
The attribution-guided pipeline does not constitute an exhaustive characterization of all computations underlying model behavior.
papers.abstract: Post-training pretrained Autoregressive models (ARMs) into Masked Diffusion models (MDMs) has emerged as a cost-effective strategy to overcome the limitations of sequential generation. However, the internal algorithmic transformations induced by this paradigm shift remain unexplored, leaving it unclear whether post-trained MDMs acquire genuine bidirectional reasoning capabilities or merely repackage autoregressive heuristics. In this work, we address this question by conducting a comparative circuit analysis of ARMs and their MDM counterparts. Our analysis reveals a systematic "mechanism shift" dependent on the structural nature of the task. Structurally, we observe a distinct divergence: while MDMs largely retain autoregressive circuitry for tasks dominated by local causal dependencies, they abandon initialized pathways for global planning tasks, exhibiting distinct rewiring characterized by increased early-layer processing. Semantically, we identify a transition from sharp, localized specialization in ARMs to distributed integration in MDMs. Through these findings, we conclude that diffusion post-training does not merely adapt model parameters but fundamentally reorganizes internal computation to support non-sequential global planning.

papers.title: Finding Highly Interpretable Prompt-Specific Circuits in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces ACC++, a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits, revealing that prompts form families with representative circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuits should be analyzed at the prompt level, and ACC++ enables scalable interpretability by identifying prompt-specific circuit families.
papers.key_findings:
ACC++ provides cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals compared to ACC.
Circuits in language models are prompt-specific, with no single circuit per task.
Prompts form clusters into families with similar circuits, allowing for representative circuits.
Signal analysis reveals stable routes and functional redundancy across prompt families.
An automated pipeline can generate interpretable explanations for circuit signals.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal circuits that language models use to solve tasks remains a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Most prior work identifies circuits at the task level by averaging across many prompts, implicitly assuming a single stable mechanism per task. We show that this assumption can obscure a crucial source of structure: circuits are prompt-specific, even within a fixed task. Building on attention causal communication (ACC) (Franco & Crovella, 2025), we introduce ACC++, refinements that extract cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals inside attention heads from a single forward pass. Like ACC, our approach does not require replacement models (e.g., SAEs) or activation patching; ACC++ further improves circuit precision by reducing attribution noise. Applying ACC++ to indirect object identification (IOI) in GPT-2, Pythia, and Gemma 2, we find there is no single circuit for IOI in any model: different prompt templates induce systematically different mechanisms. Despite this variation, prompts cluster into prompt families with similar circuits, and we propose a representative circuit for each family as a practical unit of analysis. Finally, we develop an automated interpretability pipeline that uses ACC++ signals to surface human-interpretable features and assemble mechanistic explanations for prompt families behavior. Together, our results recast circuits as a meaningful object of study by shifting the unit of analysis from tasks to prompts, enabling scalable circuit descriptions in the presence of prompt-specific mechanisms.

papers.title: Finding structure during incremental speech comprehension
papers.research_question: How does the brain incrementally construct structured interpretations during speech comprehension, and can deep language models like BERT capture this process?
papers.core_contribution: The study shows that BERT-derived incremental structural measures correlate with brain activity, revealing the neurobiological processes of incremental speech comprehension and supporting the use of deep language models as computational models for neural dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed picture of how structured interpretations are incrementally built in the brain, engaging bilateral regions, and supports the use of artificial neural networks as models for cognitive processes.
papers.key_findings:
BERT parse depths incrementally update as sentences unfold, reflecting human interpretative preferences.
BERT structural measures correlate with corpus-based lexical constraints and human behavioral data.
Neural activity in bilateral brain regions, beyond classical language areas, correlates with BERT structural measures during sentence processing.
Representational similarity analysis shows that BERT parse depth vectors fit brain activity patterns during key epochs of sentence comprehension.
The findings illustrate when and where coherent interpretations emerge in the brain through the integration of multifaceted constraints.
papers.abstract: Abstract A core aspect of human speech comprehension is the ability to incrementally integrate consecutive words into a structured and coherent interpretation, aligning with the speaker’s intended meaning. This rapid process is subject to multi-dimensional probabilistic constraints, including both linguistic knowledge and non-linguistic information within specific contexts, and it is their interpretative coherence that drives successful comprehension. To study the neural substrates of this process, we extract word-by-word measures of sentential structure from BERT, a deep language model, which effectively approximates the coherent outcomes of the dynamic interplay among various types of constraints. Using representational similarity analysis, we tested BERT parse depths and relevant corpus-based measures against the spatiotemporally resolved brain activity recorded by electro/magnetoencephalography when participants were listening to the same sentences. Our results provide a detailed picture of the neurobiological processes involved in the incremental construction of structured interpretations. These findings show when and where coherent interpretations emerge through the evaluation and integration of multifaceted constraints in the brain, which engages bilateral brain regions extending beyond the classical fronto-temporal language system. Furthermore, this study provides empirical evidence supporting the use artificial neural networks as computational models for revealing the neural dynamics underpinning complex cognitive processes in the brain.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Decomposition of Small Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Can Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) be extended to Transformer models to decompose their weights into interpretable, causally relevant subcomponents?
papers.core_contribution: Extends Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) to Transformer models by proposing a causal importance function for sequential data and a new loss function, demonstrating that SPD can recover interpretable parameter-space mechanisms in both a toy induction-head model and GPT-2-small.
papers.conclusion: Parameter decomposition can surface semantically specific mechanisms in Transformers, and SPD yields narrow, causally relevant directions that act as clean handles for mechanistic interventions.
papers.key_findings:
SPD successfully decomposes a toy induction-head model and recovers the expected 2-step copy circuit.
Applying SPD to GPT-2-small locates subcomponents corresponding to interpretable concepts like 'golf' and 'basketball'.
Ablating the recovered rank-1 slices selectively reduces the probability of the targeted fact (e.g., 'golf' for Tiger Woods) while leaving unrelated examples largely unaffected.
The method achieves a 99% size reduction in active subcomponents for the GPT-2-small fact examples compared to the full model.
Facts like athlete-sport associations can originate as early as the first MLP layer and propagate through the network.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are restricted to small-scale models, leaving open questions about scalability to larger architectures.
The causal importance parameterisation introduces additional computational overhead.
Evaluation is qualitative and task-specific, so further benchmarks are needed to establish generality across architectures and tasks.
Difficulty in establishing ground truth even for small, toy Transformers.
future_direction: Extend this work to larger models.
Improve the definition of causal importance for computations with feature interactions.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that decomposing models in parameter space may yield clean handles for analysis and intervention. Previous methods have demonstrated successful applications on a wide range of toy models, but the gap to "real models" has not yet been bridged. In this work, we extend Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) to Transformer models, proposing an updated causal importance function suited for sequential data and a new loss function. We demonstrate that SPD can successfully decompose a toy induction-head model and recover the expected 2-step circuit. We also show that applying SPD to GPT-2-small can successfully locate subcomponents corresponding to interpretable concepts like "golf" and "basketball". These results take the first step in the direction of extending SPD to modern models, and show that we can use the method to surface interpretable parameter-space mechanisms.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Incremental Processing of Principle B: Mismatches Between Neural Models and Humans
papers.research_question: Do GPT-based autoregressive neural language models use Principle B to restrict their incremental coreference processing like humans? Specifically, does Principle B block the influence of ungrammatical structural positions on pronoun prediction and cataphoric processing?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-based language models do not categorically ignore structural positions blocked by Principle B during incremental coreference processing, unlike humans. This mismatch suggests that certain aspects of human parsing behavior are not directly evidenced in linguistic data and may relate to properties of the training data.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive neural models do not uniformly process pronouns like humans; they fail to capture qualitative patterns of incremental coreference processing and underestimate processing costs. Models appear to learn only those aspects of Principle B that have predictable reflexes in training data.
papers.key_findings:
For object pronouns (him) in positions where Principle B blocks co-indexation, all models exhibited a negative Gender Mismatch Effect (GMME), meaning they expected the pronoun to mismatch in gender with the grammatically unavailable antecedent.
For possessive pronouns (his), all models showed positive GMMEs across all structural positions, expecting gender agreement with antecedents.
In cataphoric object pronoun processing, larger models (GPT-J and GPT-3) showed no significant GMME when Principle B blocked coreference, aligning with human behavior, while smaller models (GPT-2 XL and GPT-Neo) showed a positive GMME.
Neural models greatly underestimate the magnitude of processing costs observed in humans, even in cases of qualitative overlap.
Analysis of the training data (the Pile) reveals a surface distribution bias where pronouns are more likely to mismatch in gender with antecedents in positions blocked by Principle B, suggesting models may overfit this pattern.
papers.limitation:
Whether models truly 'interpret' the correct coreference relations is unclear; techniques are limited for assessing if models comprehend meaning in a human-like fashion.
The study relies on stereotypical associations between nouns and pronouns, which does not cleanly map onto the real world (e.g., singular they is not considered).
The investigation is limited to English, due to resource availability and the focus of existing psycholinguistic work, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Future work might consider analyses of the attention mechanisms to dig deeper into what information models are using.
papers.abstract: Despite neural language models qualitatively capturing many human linguistic behaviors, recent work has demonstrated that they underestimate the true processing costs of ungrammatical structures. We extend these more fine-grained comparisons between humans and models by investigating the interaction between Principle B and coreference processing. While humans use Principle B to block certain structural positions from affecting their incremental processing, we find that GPT-based language models are influenced by ungrammatical positions. We conclude by relating the mismatch between neural models and humans to properties of training data and suggest that certain aspects of human processing behavior do not directly follow from linguistic data.Paper at CoNLL 2022

papers.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
papers.research_question: How does the in-context learning capability emerge in transformers, specifically for learning Markov chains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ICL-MC task as a controlled setting to study in-context learning, showing transformers learn 'statistical induction heads' through phase transitions, and that simplicity bias can delay learning the optimal solution.
papers.conclusion: The ICL-MC task provides a useful controlled setting for understanding in-context learning and the emergence of statistical induction heads, revealing that networks pass through discrete incomplete solutions which may affect the speed of learning more complex circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn statistical induction heads to optimally solve the in-context Markov chain task.
Learning occurs in phases: an initial uniform phase, a unigram phase, and a final bigram phase with a rapid transition between them.
The model's bias towards simpler (unigram) solutions can slow down the learning of the optimal bigram solution.
The alignment between the transformer's layers is crucial for the phase transition to the correct solution.
During training, positional embeddings develop an alternating pattern, with a bias towards looking back an odd number of tokens.
future_direction: Investigate how the presence of simple incomplete solutions affects the formation of more complex circuits in language modeling and other rich learning settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models have the ability to generate text that mimics patterns in their inputs. We introduce a simple Markov Chain sequence modeling task in order to study how this in-context learning (ICL) capability emerges. In our setting, each example is sampled from a Markov chain drawn from a prior distribution over Markov chains. Transformers trained on this task form \emph{statistical induction heads} which compute accurate next-token probabilities given the bigram statistics of the context. During the course of training, models pass through multiple phases: after an initial stage in which predictions are uniform, they learn to sub-optimally predict using in-context single-token statistics (unigrams); then, there is a rapid phase transition to the correct in-context bigram solution. We conduct an empirical and theoretical investigation of this multi-phase process, showing how successful learning results from the interaction between the transformer's layers, and uncovering evidence that the presence of the simpler unigram solution may delay formation of the final bigram solution. We examine how learning is affected by varying the prior distribution over Markov chains, and consider the generalization of our in-context learning of Markov chains (ICL-MC) task to $n$-grams for $n > 2$.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s "Interpretability Illusion" Arguments
papers.research_question: Are the phenomena identified by Makelov et al. (2023) as 'interpretability illusions' actually inherent properties of distributed representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the 'interpretability illusions' identified by Makelov et al. (2023) are not illusions but inherent properties of distributed representations, and provides additional experiments using DAS to analyze causal mechanisms in GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: The phenomena labeled as 'interpretability illusions' are inherent to distributed representations, and the work by Makelov et al. (2023) has advanced the field of mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Even directions considered non-illusory by Makelov et al. can be classified as illusory under their own definition.
The illusions reported by Makelov et al. are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms.
DAS can reproduce and extend findings on the IOI task, showing that name position information in GPT-2 is distributed across attention heads and emerges in the 8th layer.
Name position information is not carried by MLP activations but by the self-attention block in the 8th layer.
The correct IO name representation is distributed across multiple attention heads in the 9th layer.
papers.abstract: We respond to the recent paper by Makelov et al. (2023), which reviews subspace interchange intervention methods like distributed alignment search (DAS; Geiger et al. 2023) and claims that these methods potentially cause "interpretability illusions". We first review Makelov et al. (2023)'s technical notion of what an "interpretability illusion" is, and then we show that even intuitive and desirable explanations can qualify as illusions in this sense. As a result, their method of discovering "illusions" can reject explanations they consider "non-illusory". We then argue that the illusions Makelov et al. (2023) see in practice are artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms. We close by emphasizing that, though we disagree with their core characterization, Makelov et al. (2023)'s examples and discussion have undoubtedly pushed the field of interpretability forward.

papers.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reasoning performance consistently improve as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes grow longer, and what is the optimal CoT length?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that an optimal Chain-of-Thought length exists, following an inverted U-shaped curve with performance, and that this optimal length scales with task difficulty and model capability, revealing a simplicity bias where more capable models prefer shorter CoTs.
papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Memorization Recall Through Idioms
papers.research_question: When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodological framework and dataset for probing memorization recall in transformers, and finds that memorized predictions involve a two-step process of candidate promotion in early layers and confidence boosting in upper layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence.
Memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network.
The first layer is especially critical for memorized predictions.
The findings generalize from idioms to factual statements.
The IDIO MEM dataset is constructed for probing memorization and released for the community.
papers.abstract: To produce accurate predictions, language models (LMs) must balance between generalization and memorization. Yet, little is known about the mechanism by which transformer LMs employ their memorization capacity. When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory? In this work, we offer the first methodological framework for probing and characterizing recall of memorized sequences in transformer LMs. First, we lay out criteria for detecting model inputs that trigger memory recall, and propose idioms as inputs that typically fulfill these criteria. Next, we construct a dataset of English idioms and use it to compare model behavior on memorized vs. non-memorized inputs. Specifically, we analyze the internal prediction construction process by interpreting the model's hidden representations as a gradual refinement of the output probability distribution. We find that across different model sizes and architectures, memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence. This suggests that memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network. Last, we demonstrate the utility of our methodology beyond idioms in memorized factual statements. Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.

papers.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning emerge in transformers, and what are the inner workings and conditions for its appearance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers through the identification and analysis of a specialized attention mechanism called an 'iteration head', which enables efficient iterative reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve iterative tasks efficiently via CoT reasoning by developing inner circuits (iteration heads) dedicated to multistep reasoning, and data curation can guide this process.
papers.key_findings:
Iteration heads, a specific pattern of weights in the first two attention layers, emerge in transformers trained on iterative tasks with CoT.
These heads enable the transformer to solve iterative tasks efficiently by retrieving the current input and previous state to compute the next state.
The iterative reasoning skill granted by iteration heads is transferable between different iterative tasks (e.g., from copying to parity).
Data curation (including easier tasks in training) can guide the model towards learning the iteration head circuit.
Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a limitation for complex iterative algorithms.
papers.limitation: Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a shortcoming for complex iterative algorithms or generic language modeling.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power. However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited. This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting. In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads". We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
